purpose: This tool lets you race two ways of growing: adding the same amount each period and multiplying by the same amount. You see why multiplying always wins in the end, and how decay works.

stops.title: Blue against red
stops.text: The blue curve multiplies each period. The red line adds the same amount each period. A dashed vertical line marks the time you are reading, with a dot on each curve and its value. Nothing on the picture is draggable.
stops.try: Use the Read at time t slider and watch the two dots separate.

stops.title: Start amount
stops.text: How much there is at time 0. It scales both curves. A bigger start does not change how fast the blue curve pulls away in percent terms.
stops.try: Set it to 100, then look at the axis numbers.

stops.title: Growth per period
stops.text: The percent added each period. At 100 percent the amount doubles. Negative values make decay, and the readout then shows a half-life instead of a doubling time.
stops.try: Slide it below 0 and watch the blue curve fall but never reach 0.

stops.title: Read at time t
stops.text: Moves the dashed line and updates the readout below. Periods shown, just above, sets how long the timeline runs. Waiting longer reveals how far the curves part.
stops.try: Slide to 3.5 and compare the two values in the readout.

stops.title: Linear comparison
stops.text: Shows or hides the red line that adds the same amount each period. Hide it to see the curve on its own, with a better scale.
stops.try: Switch it off, then on again.

stops.title: Quick presets
stops.text: Doubling, 10% growth and 30% decay set up the three cases from the steps. They animate the sliders to those settings.

stops.title: What Next does
stops.text: Each step loads one of those cases with the story: add versus multiply, a longer wait, a small percent, then decay.

stops.title: Quick check
stops.text: A short exit ticket with reasons after each answer.

teacher: Project step 2 with 20 periods and ask students to predict both values before you read them. Ask: why does a small percent still win eventually? Misconception: thinking growth of 10 percent means adding 10 each time, which the red line shows is different.
